lesson.title: Am Tisch: die Gabel, das Messer, die Flasche, der Becher, die Kanne
lesson.subtitle: a knife that is literally a meat-saw, and three words Latin handed to both languages

hook.title: The Knife Is a Meat-Saw
hook.content: das Messer is the oldest compound at the table: Proto-Germanic *matisahsą, built from *mati, 'food' — the exact word English meat comes from, which originally meant food of any kind — plus *sahs, 'blade', the word Old Norse preserved as sax. German shifted food's T to a Z (mati → mezzi, the zehn/two shift) and squeezed the compound down to Messer. The knife literally is a meat-blade. die Flasche and English flask are the same Germanic word, *flaska — but English had to borrow its own word BACK through Medieval Latin flasco, a boomerang loan. der Becher is Latin bicarium, which English borrowed as beaker; die Kanne most likely goes back to Latin canna, 'reed', the little tube that became German Kanne and English can — the standard guess, though not a settled fact. die Gabel is the honest loss: pure Germanic *gabulō, with no English twin — English took 'fork' from Latin furca instead.

footnotes.title: Meat Once Meant Food
footnotes.content: In Old English, mete meant food in general — 'sweetmeats', originally, were just sweets. So *matisahsą was not a 'meat-knife' in the modern sense; it was simply the food-knife, the blade you cut dinner with. German compressed the whole idea into seven letters: Messer.

pattern.title: Pouring, Cutting, Counting
pattern.content: 1. aus for what comes out: Ich trinke den Kaffee aus dem Becher — aus + dem, the drink leaves the vessel. 2. in for what goes in: Das Wasser ist in der Flasche — in + der, the water stays put. 3. Hot things get a warning frame: Einen Moment, bitte, die Kanne ist heiß — einen because der Moment is masculine accusative, bitte because politeness is free. 4. Counting the table: Die Zahl ist vier (the number is four), and the numeral again takes the bare plural — vier Teller, vier Gabeln, no article. 5. The half: Die Hälfte der Teller ist hier — die Hälfte governs the genitive, and the verb agrees with the singular Hälfte, not the plural Teller.
pattern.linguist_note: The standard guess: Latin canna 'reed' gave Germanic *kannō, 'small container' — perhaps, not proven. English kept it tiny (can), German made it elegant (die Kanne) — and if the guess holds, both languages still pour from the same Latin reed.

exercises.prompt: Am Tisch — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: A moment please, the pot is hot
matching_pairs.german: Einen Moment, bitte, die Kanne ist heiß

matching_pairs.english: The water is in the bottle
matching_pairs.german: Das Wasser ist in der Flasche

matching_pairs.english: I drink the coffee from the mug
matching_pairs.german: Ich trinke den Kaffee aus dem Becher

matching_pairs.english: Half of the plates are here
matching_pairs.german: Die Hälfte der Teller ist hier

matching_pairs.english: The fork and the knife are on the table
matching_pairs.german: Die Gabel und das Messer sind auf dem Tisch

exercises.target_answer: Einen Moment, bitte, die Kanne ist heiß, Das Wasser ist in der Flasche, Ich trinke den Kaffee aus dem Becher, Die Hälfte der Teller ist hier, Die Zahl ist vier, Die Gabel und das Messer sind auf dem Tisch
exercises.meaning: a hot pot and a polite warning, water in the bottle, coffee from the mug, half the plates here, the number four, fork and knife on the table
exercises.explanation: The table set in six sentences. in der Flasche is dative because the water rests there; aus dem Becher is dative because the coffee only leaves it; and die Gabel und das Messer shows the gender flip — die, then das — with no warning.

exercises.prompt: Which of these table words wears the T→Z badge that turned *mati into mezzi-, food into meat's German twin?
exercises.meaning: messer's first half wears the T→Z badge: *mati → mezzi
exercises.explanation: das Messer is ancient *matisahsą: *mati 'food' + *sahs 'blade'. English meat kept the T of *mati; German hardened it to a Z-sound, exactly as in zwei/two and zehn/ten. The second half, *sahs 'blade', survives intact in Old Norse sax — the meat-saw that became das Messer. die Flasche, der Becher and die Kanne wear no shift badge; they are loans.

exercises.prompt: der Becher is German's version of Latin bicarium — give the English word borrowed from the same Latin:
exercises.meaning: der Becher ↔ beaker — both from Latin bicarium
exercises.explanation: Latin bicarium served both languages: German took der Becher straight, English took beaker (and via Old Norse, bikarr). The same Latin poured die Flasche's cousin flask back into English and turned die Kanne's reed into a can.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the warning: 'A moment please, the pot is hot'
exercises.target_answer: Einen Moment, bitte, die Kanne ist heiß
exercises.meaning: A moment please, the pot is hot
exercises.explanation: der Moment is masculine, so the accusative warning takes einen — a giveaway that English 'moment' never had. bitte softens it, and die Kanne ist heiß closes with the dangerous fact. The tiles Teller and Wasser are decoys from the rest of the table.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'The number is four and the half is two'
exercises.target_answer: Die Zahl ist vier und die Hälfte ist zwei
exercises.meaning: The number is four and the half is two
exercises.explanation: Setting the table with Zählen-I and Zählen-II grammar: die Zahl announces the count, die Hälfte halves it — vier Teller, zwei Gabeln — and the numeral again takes the bare plural with no article. The Teller and Gabeln in the bank are the pieces waiting to be counted.

summary.outcome: Set a table in German: pour from die Kanne, drink aus dem Becher, warn politely about what is heiß — and count die Zahl with bare plurals.

use_example.german: Einen Moment, bitte — die Kanne ist heiß, und die Zahl ist vier: vier Teller, vier Gabeln.
use_example.english: A moment please — the pot is hot, and the number is four: four plates, four forks.

summary.takeaway: Messer is *matisahsą, the meat-saw (meat + the T→Z shift), Flasche and flask are one boomerang word, Becher and beaker share bicarium, Kanne and can probably share canna — and die Gabel stands alone, honestly.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the kitchen's real estate — der Herd, der Ofen, die Seife, der Kamm, die Klingel — and a word that really is oven's twin, with an f where English wears a v.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Am Tisch: die Gabel, das Messer, die Flasche, der Becher, die Kanne (The number is four and the half is two):
twist.target_answer: Die Zahl ist vier und die Hälfte ist zwei
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Die Zahl ist vier und die Hälfte ist zwei" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Am Tisch: die Gabel, das Messer, die Flasche, der Becher, die Kanne without relying on short-term echo.

gabel.context_phrase: Ich esse den Salat mit der Gabel.
gabel.context_translation: I am eating the salad with the fork.
gabel.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic gabulu, meaning fork; English gable is the same Germanic word, naming the fork-shaped upper end of a house wall. [wiktionary]

messer.context_phrase: Schneide das Brot mit dem Messer.
messer.context_translation: Cut the bread with the knife.
messer.etymology_derivation: From Old High German mezzisahs, literally food knife; the first part is the food root behind English meat, the second the knife root behind English saw, with t appearing as ss in German. [wiktionary]

flasche.context_phrase: Die Flasche Wasser kostet zwei Euro.
flasche.context_translation: The bottle of water costs two euros.
flasche.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic flasko, from a root meaning to plait or braid, since bottles were once wrapped in straw; English flask is a direct cognate. [wiktionary]

becher.context_phrase: Ich trinke den Kakao aus einem Becher.
becher.context_translation: I am drinking the cocoa from a mug.
becher.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic bikari, borrowed from Latin bicarium, likely a diminutive of Greek bikos, meaning jar or amphora; English beaker is the same Latin loan. [wiktionary]

kanne.context_phrase: Die Kanne Tee ist noch heiß.
kanne.context_translation: The pot of tea is still hot.
kanne.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic kanno; English can is a direct cognate from Old English canne, originally meaning cup or vessel. [wiktionary]

zahl.context_phrase: Die Zahl sieben ist meine Glückszahl.
zahl.context_translation: The number seven is my lucky number.
zahl.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *talō — the entry lists English tale as a cognate, the same tal-root as tell; the initial t became z. [wiktionary]

hälfte.context_phrase: Ich esse nur die Hälfte des Kuchens.
hälfte.context_translation: I eat only half of the cake.
hälfte.etymology_derivation: halb + the deadjectival suffix -te — the twin of half; the entry notes the old b ↔ ft alternation was never levelled. [wiktionary]

moment.etymology_derivation: From Latin momentum — the same Latin loan as English moment. [wiktionary]

teller.etymology_derivation: From Middle French tailloir, meaning cutting board, from the Old French cutting verb tailler; English tailor descends from the same Old French verb. [wiktionary]

tisch.context_phrase: Der Teller steht auf dem Tisch.
tisch.context_translation: The plate stands on the table.
tisch.etymology_derivation: Latin discus → Old English disc (dish/desk) → Old High German tisc (tisch, with d → t).

salzig.etymology_derivation: salzig — from Salz (salt) plus -ig; the old t survives in English salt but shifted to z in German Salz, the Sibilant Shift at work. [wiktionary]

anzug.context_phrase: Er trägt einen schwarzen Anzug zur Arbeit.
anzug.context_translation: He wears a black suit to work.
anzug.etymology_derivation: an- + Zug (a pulling); Zug descends from Proto-Germanic *tugiz, the exact twin of English tug - the suit you pull on. [wiktionary]

zäh.context_translation: The old chewing gum is tough.
zäh.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *tą̄h(ī) — English tough is the documented cognate; English kept the t and spelled the gh, German shifted t to z and lost the h. Doublet of German taff. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
